sampling_model.design: Uniform assignment over \(\mathcal Z_n\), the assignments treating exactly \(m=n/2\) units.
sampling_model.units: The \(n\) labeled units and both binary potential outcomes are fixed; the assignment is the only randomness.
sampling_model.treatment: One binary treatment with exactly \(m\) treated and \(m\) controls.
sampling_model.overlap: Every labeled exactly balanced assignment has probability \(1/\binom n m\).
sampling_model.nuisance_estimation: There is no stochastic nuisance estimation; nature ranges over the finite response-type state space \(\mathcal N_n\).

comparator_promise_table.comparator_claim: ``Independent random assignment remains optimal, and the generally-nonlinear optimal estimator can meaningfully reduce worst-case MSE.''
``For binary potential outcomes, we show this minimax risk is equivalent to the minimax risk of an estimation problem with \(2\) unknown parameters.''
``A new proof of this result is given, and the restriction to experiments with a finite number of outcomes is removed.''
``This paper shows the minimax optimality of the complete randomization scheme under permutation invariance.''

body.tldr: Exact balance removes treatment-share variation but leaves two observed arm-success counts. For fixed binary potential outcomes, the full pair and its difference have the same worst-schedule ATE squared-error minimax risk at \(n=2,4,6\), including a seven-state algebraic saddle at six, but they separate at \(n=8\). A rational full-count rule and a rational difference-only prior certify \(\rho_8^{\mathrm{CR}}<0.06541<0.06578<\rho_8^W\), so eight is the first size at which the second count has minimax value. Later-size persistence and every asymptotic law for the compression tax remain open.

project_justification.gap: Published minimax analyses either optimize unrestricted assignment through a shifted-binomial reduction or study complete randomization with affine or prescribed estimators. Exact binary randomization-inference papers retain the observed table but do not compare unrestricted point-estimation risk with the risk after compressing it to the difference.
project_justification.niche: The fixed-half response-type hypergeometric experiment is a finite decision problem in which Blackwell weak dominance is automatic, yet strict value for ATE squared loss depends on the least-favorable posterior geometry.
project_justification.fill: The project gives analytic primal and least-favorable-prior equality certificates at \(n=2,4,6\), a complete algebraic verification at six, and a serialized rational upper-lower separation at eight, thereby locating the first exact failure of the scalar reduction.

body.related_work: Hull (2026, Theorem 1, Proposition 2, and footnote 12) shows that bounded outcomes can reverse familiar design prescriptions, proves complete-randomization suboptimality for an affine class, and leaves general-estimator complete-randomization strictness conjectural; it motivates but does not subsume the within-design count-compression question here. Sudijono, Dobriban, and Tchetgen Tchetgen (2026, Theorems 2.1--2.2 and 3.1) reduce the unrestricted binary design-estimator game to a shifted-binomial experiment and derive nonlinear shrinkage and the Airy correction. For the finite problem here, their independent scalar likelihood is replaced by the exact two-count kernel derived in Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}response\mbox{-}type\mbox{-}minimax\mbox{-}games}\); a uniform boundary expansion comparing that kernel with its projection remains open. Ding and Dasgupta (2016, Table 1, equation (1), and Section 2) supply the four response types and the observed two-by-two table used to derive that kernel. Blackwell (1953) implies that the full count pair weakly dominates its deterministic compression, but not that the inequality is strict for this one estimand and loss. Bai (2023, Theorems 3.1--3.3) establishes complete-randomization and Neyman-allocation results in a permutation-invariant linear framework, leaving arbitrary nonlinear rules over fixed binary schedules outside its scope. Rigdon and Hudgens (2015) and Li and Ding (2016) use the full binary table for exact confidence sets; they neither study minimax point estimation nor license a confidence-set claim here. Li and Ding (2017) provide first-order finite-population limit tools, not the finite threshold or higher-order information loss.
body.technical_internal_limitation: A prior can make the second count strictly Bayes-informative at \(n=4\) and \(n=6\) even though the minimax values are equal. Thus posterior relevance under an arbitrary prior cannot prove strict minimax separation. The \(n=8\) action is only a feasible full-count upper certificate, and the \(n=8\) prior is only a difference-game lower certificate; neither exact minimax value at eight is claimed.
body.honest_scope: The finite response-type games, equality at \(n=2,4,6\), strict separation at \(n=8\), and the first-lossy-size conclusion are theorem-level targets. The paper makes no confidence-set claim, no pointwise-dominance claim, and no assertion that \(t_8\) is exact minimax. Strictness for any even \(n\ge10\), every power law or constant for \(\Delta_n\), parity-dependent limits, and all higher-order balance-tax statements remain open. The standard special-case check is exact: at \(n=2\), both experiments reduce to the displayed three-state saddle with value \(1/4\).
